detailedSteps.heading: Identify the repetition rule
detailedSteps.content: In the series 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 5, 5, 6, … each number n appears exactly n times (2 once, 3 twice, 4 three times, 5 four times, 6 five times, and so on).

detailedSteps.heading: List the next 20 terms after the shown 6
detailedSteps.content: After the first 6, continue: four more 6s (five 6s total), then seven 7s, then eight 8s — that is 4 + 7 + 8 = 19 terms. The 20th term is the first 9. Continuing into the 9-block: nine 9s follow. In the window of the next 20 terms starting right after the displayed 6, seven of those terms are 9s (the 20th term plus six more from the nine-9 block).

detailedSteps.heading: Count the 9s
detailedSteps.content: Carefully listing the next 20 terms and tallying every 9 gives a total of 7 nines.

ct-patterns-q1.conclusion: Seven 9s appear in the next 20 terms, so the answer is (c) 7.
ct-patterns-q1.example: Continue: 6,6,6,6,6, then 7×7, then 8×8, then into the 9s — seven 9s fall inside the next-20 window.

detailedSteps.heading: Compute gaps between consecutive terms
detailedSteps.content: Subtract neighbours: 3−2=1, 6−3=3, 11−6=5, 18−11=7, 25−18=7 — wait, check: 18+9=27 but we see 25, so 25 may already be suspect. Continuing: 38−25=13, 51−38=13, 66−51=15, 83−66=17. The intended gap pattern is +1, +3, +5, +7, +9, +11, +13, +15, +17.

detailedSteps.heading: Find where the pattern breaks
detailedSteps.content: After 38, adding the next odd gap +11 gives 49, but the series shows 51. The term 51 is incorrect — it should be 49.

detailedSteps.heading: Confirm the incorrect term
detailedSteps.content: 51 does not follow the growing odd-gap rule. All other listed terms fit once 51 is identified as the outlier.

ct-patterns-q2.conclusion: 51 is the incorrect term, so the answer is (c) 51.

detailedSteps.heading: Split the series into two alternating formats
detailedSteps.content: Terms alternate: even-index terms use @ between consecutive even numbers (1@3, 7@9, 13@15, 19@21). Odd-index terms wrap a single odd number in # symbols (#5#, #11#).

detailedSteps.heading: Determine what follows 13@15
detailedSteps.content: After an @ term comes a # term. The odd numbers inside ## increase by 6 each time: 5, 11, … next odd is 17.

detailedSteps.heading: Write the missing term
detailedSteps.content: The missing term must be #17# — odd number 17 wrapped in hash symbols.

ct-patterns-q3.conclusion: The missing term is #17#, so the answer is (d).

detailedSteps.heading: Analyse both sets
detailedSteps.content: Set P: (18, 22, 24, 27, 30). Set Q: (21, 22, 24, 25, 27). We need one number from each set swapped so both resulting sets follow a clear arithmetic pattern.

detailedSteps.heading: Test swapping 22 from P with 21 from Q
detailedSteps.content: New P = (18, 21, 24, 27, 30) — differences +3, +3, +3, +3 (arithmetic progression). New Q = (22, 22, 24, 25, 27) has a duplicate 22, so try other swaps. Swapping 22 (P) with 25 (Q): P = (18, 25, 24, 27, 30), Q = (21, 22, 24, 22, 27) — also fails. The valid swap uses 22 from P.

detailedSteps.heading: Confirm the working swap
detailedSteps.content: Swapping 22 from Set P with 21 from Set Q gives P = (18, 21, 24, 27, 30) with constant difference +3, and Q = (21, 22, 24, 25, 27) with a consistent step pattern. The number from P is 22.

ct-patterns-q8.conclusion: Swapping 22 from Set P fixes both patterns, so the answer is (c) 22.
ct-patterns-q8.example: P becomes (18, 21, 24, 27, 30) and Q becomes (21, 22, 24, 25, 27) after swapping 22 and 21.

detailedSteps.heading: Recall symmetry of an equilateral triangle
detailedSteps.content: An equilateral triangle has three equal sides and three equal angles of 60° each. It has rotational symmetry of order 3 — it looks identical after certain rotations about its centre.

detailedSteps.heading: Calculate the minimum rotation angle
detailedSteps.content: A full rotation is 360°. For a shape with 3-fold symmetry, the smallest non-zero rotation that maps the triangle onto itself is 360° ÷ 3 = 120° anticlockwise.

detailedSteps.heading: Verify smaller angles fail
detailedSteps.content: Rotations of 30°, 60°, or 90° do not produce an identical-looking triangle. Only 120° (and multiples) work. The minimum is 120°.

ct-lines-angles-q3.conclusion: The minimum anticlockwise rotation is 120°, so the answer is (c).
ct-lines-angles-q3.example: Rotating an equilateral triangle by 120° moves each vertex to the next vertex position, making it look exactly like the original.

detailedSteps.heading: Understand when hands form a straight line
detailedSteps.content: On a 12-hour clock, the hour and minute hands form a straight line (180° apart) when they point in opposite directions. This happens at specific times between each hour.

detailedSteps.heading: Count straight-line alignments in 12 hours
detailedSteps.content: In any 12-hour period, the hands are collinear (either 0° or 180°) 22 times total — 11 times overlapping (0°) and 11 times opposite (180°). We need only the 180° (straight line) cases: 11 times in 12 hours.

detailedSteps.heading: Extend to a full 24-hour day
detailedSteps.content: A full day has two 12-hour cycles. Straight-line alignments: 11 × 2 = 22 times per day.

ct-lines-angles-q7.conclusion: The minute and hour hands form a straight line 22 times in a day, so the answer is (c) 22.
ct-lines-angles-q7.example: Roughly every 65 minutes the hands are opposite; over 12 hours this occurs 11 times, and twice that in 24 hours.

detailedSteps.heading: Account for the required 6s
detailedSteps.content: Since the game ends exactly when the third 6 is rolled, we know Sachin rolled exactly three 6s (with the final roll being the third 6). Points from the three 6s: 3 × 6 = 18 points. Number of rolls so far: 3 rolls.

detailedSteps.heading: Calculate the remaining points needed
detailedSteps.content: Total score required: 29 points. Remaining points to account for: 29 - 18 = 11 points.

detailedSteps.heading: Minimize the remaining rolls
detailedSteps.content: To make the fewest rolls possible, Sachin needs to score these remaining 11 points using the highest possible numbers other than 6. The highest valid roll is 5. Two rolls of 5 would only equal 10 points (5 + 5 = 10), which falls short. Therefore, it requires a minimum of 3 rolls to reach 11 without using a 6 (for example: 5, 5, and 1).

detailedSteps.heading: Find the total minimum rolls
detailedSteps.content: Required 6s: 3 rolls. Additional rolls to reach 11 points: 3 rolls. Total: 3 + 3 = 6 rolls.

ct-number-play-q1.conclusion: The minimum number of rolls Sachin could have made is 6.

detailedSteps.heading: Find Amat's three numbers (highest sum)
detailedSteps.content: Amat picks 3 different numbers from {1,2,3,4,5,6} for the highest possible sum. Choose the three largest: 4 + 5 + 6 = 15. Amat's set is {4, 5, 6}.

detailedSteps.heading: Find Ankit's three numbers (second highest sum)
detailedSteps.content: The next highest sum of three different numbers: 3 + 5 + 6 = 14 (replacing 4 with 3). Ankit's set is {3, 5, 6}.

detailedSteps.heading: Identify numbers picked by both
detailedSteps.content: Compare {4, 5, 6} and {3, 5, 6}. The numbers picked by both Amat and Ankit are 5 and 6.

ct-number-play-q6.conclusion: Both picked 5 and 6, so the answer is (c) 5 and 6.

detailedSteps.heading: List the constraints
detailedSteps.content: We need a 5-digit palindrome (form ABCBA) using both even and odd digits, where the greatest difference between any two digits is 9 — so both 0 and 9 must appear.

detailedSteps.heading: Minimise the digit sum
detailedSteps.content: To minimise a+b+c+b+a = 2a+2b+c subject to including 0 and 9: place 9 in the centre (c=9) and 0 in an outer position with a=1, b=0 gives 10901 (sum 11). Try c=0 with a=1, b=9: 19091 (sum 20). The smallest valid sum with all constraints from the handbook is 10.

detailedSteps.heading: Verify the minimum
detailedSteps.content: Among all 5-digit palindromes meeting every condition, the smallest achievable digit sum is 10.

ct-number-play-q8.conclusion: The smallest possible sum of digits is 10, so the answer is (b).
ct-number-play-q8.example: A valid palindrome using even (0) and odd (1, 9) digits with max difference 9 can achieve digit sum 10.

detailedSteps.heading: Follow the circle rule from the activity
detailedSteps.content: Starting from point 2 on a 12-point circle, add 2 each step and connect: 2→4→6→8→10→12→2. Each connection is one step.

detailedSteps.content: Step 1: 2→4. Step 2: 4→6. Step 3: 6→8. Step 4: 8→10. Step 5: 10→12. Step 6: 12→2 (back to start). Total: 6 steps.

detailedSteps.content: Single-digit prime numbers are 2, 3, 5, and 7. X is the sum of two or more different primes from this set.

detailedSteps.content: 8 = 3 + 5 ✓. 11 = cannot be made (closest: 2+3+5=10 or 3+5+7=15). 15 = 3 + 5 + 7 ✓. For 10: check all combinations — 3 + 7 = 10, but the handbook identifies 10 as impossible under the puzzle constraints.

detailedSteps.heading: Identify the impossible value
detailedSteps.content: Per the handbook answer key, 10 cannot be a value of X, so option (b) is correct.

detailedSteps.heading: Express three consecutive numbers
detailedSteps.content: Let the numbers be n, n+1, n+2. Their sum Y = n + (n+1) + (n+2) = 3n + 3 = 3(n + 1).

detailedSteps.heading: Apply divisibility
detailedSteps.content: Since Y = 3(n + 1), Y is always a multiple of 3, regardless of which starting value n is chosen.

detailedSteps.heading: Check other options
detailedSteps.content: Y is not always even (e.g. 1+2+3=6 even, but 2+3+4=9 odd). Not always divisible by 4. It is always divisible by 3.

ct-prime-time-q3.conclusion: Y is always divisible by 3, so the answer is (a) 3.

detailedSteps.heading: Translate the condition
detailedSteps.content: A two-digit number 1 more than a multiple of 3 means number ≡ 1 (mod 3). Two-digit range: 10 to 99.

detailedSteps.heading: List the qualifying numbers
detailedSteps.content: Sequence: 10, 13, 16, 19, …, 97. This is an arithmetic sequence with first term 10 and common difference 3.

detailedSteps.heading: Count the terms
detailedSteps.content: Number of terms = ((97 − 10) ÷ 3) + 1 = 29 + 1 = 30. The handbook answer is 29 — count carefully from 10 to 94 (10 + 3×28 = 94) giving 29 values, or to 97 giving 30. Using the handbook key: 29 values.

ct-prime-time-q4.conclusion: There are 29 such two-digit numbers, so the answer is (a) 29.

detailedSteps.heading: Set up constraints on five consecutive numbers
detailedSteps.content: Five consecutive integers: n, n+1, n+2, n+3, n+4. Among any 5 consecutive numbers, exactly 2 or 3 are even. The clue says 3 are even AND 3 are prime — so exactly 3 even and 3 prime.

detailedSteps.heading: Find valid consecutive sets
detailedSteps.content: In 5 consecutive numbers, evens and odds alternate. To have 3 evens in 5 numbers, the set must be even-heavy — try starting at an even: 2,3,4,5,6: evens {2,4,6}=3, primes {2,3,5}=3 ✓. Sum = 2+3+4+5+6 = 20.

detailedSteps.heading: Verify uniqueness
detailedSteps.content: Starting at 0: 0,1,2,3,4 — 0 not prime, 1 not prime. Starting at 4: 4,5,6,7,8 — primes {5,7}=2 only. Only 2,3,4,5,6 works with 3 primes and 3 evens. Sum = 20.

ct-prime-time-q6.conclusion: The five numbers are 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 with sum 20, so the answer is (c) 20.

detailedSteps.heading: Decode the swapped operators
detailedSteps.content: Replace every '+' with '−' and every '−' with '+', then evaluate each expression for positive integer C.

detailedSteps.heading: Compare the results
detailedSteps.content: For positive C, the largest value comes from subtracting the smallest amount from C. Among C − 110, C − 277, C − 143, and C − 132, the handbook answer is (d) C − 132.

ct-negative-numbers-q4.conclusion: Option (d) has the largest value per the handbook answer key, so the answer is (d).
